rationale:
Mara Voss, read as FIELD MEDIC in one second by stacking seven independent role cues down the figure: a pushed-up headlamp with a lit lens, bone collar piping, canvas apron bib-straps over the shoulders, a bone cross stencilled on a rust chest bib, a bandolier of teal ampoules at the waist, a slung med-case her left hand is plunged into, and an oversized muzzle-up injector with a visible charge window clamped in her right fist. Proportions are 3.3 heads (head rows 2-19 = 18px; figure rows 2-61 = 60px) with a 20px-wide head, thin limbs and deliberately huge mitten hands - chibi hero, not naturalistic. THIS PASS IS RENDERING AND PALETTE ONLY: the silhouette, pose and cue set are byte-identical to the previous version (0 pixels of mask drift, 0 outline-ink pixels moved - both machine-checked on every build). What changed is that the figure used to be 24 flat colour fields and is now 55 colours arranged as nine material ramps.

The ramps are skin (6 steps, L46-215), hair (5, L24-109), canvas (6, L51-186), bone (5, L108-245), rust (7, L35-196), coat (6, L28-147), steel (5, L45-185), teal (6, L37-244) and leather (5, L23-103), plus three cross-material grime tones - #4e4536 dried mud, #7c6a4e road dust, #7a5342 oxide bloom - and #120b10 plum-black, still the deepest ink anchor by a clear margin (L14, next darkest L23). No magenta, no chartreuse; the nearest colour in the sheet sits 94 RGB units from #ff2e6c and 103 from #c8f031.

Every ramp carries a hue rotation, not just a value ramp: shadows swing cool and lights swing warm. Skin goes #3e252e plum-cool at the terminator through #b87c58 base to #f2d3a6 golden on the cheekbone. Canvas folds to a slate #32313e and lifts to a sandy #c8b997. Bone shades to a grey-violet #6d6a74 and peaks at a warm off-white #fbf5e6. Rust drops to a plum-black oxide #37191f and bleaches to #eeba85 on the bib's top-left corner. That means shadow-side pixels across four different materials share a violet cast and lit-side pixels share a gold cast, which is what makes the separate objects read as lit by one lamp.

The key light is upper-left, consistent with the rest of the set, and it is applied by two separate signals rather than one, because collapsing them is exactly what makes rule-shaded pixel art look noisy. A silhouette-depth term (how far a pixel sits under the true outer edge, measured by a ray toward the upper-left that ignores interior ink) turns broad masses; a seam term (distance to the nearest interior ink line - a strap, a panel edge, a buckle) adds a smaller secondary lift, so hard corners catch a rim without the whole field blowing out. Two low-frequency terms across x and down y keep large flats turning even away from any edge. Per-material gain then decides how much of that a surface is allowed: steel takes 1.15 and shows a hard specular, bone takes only 0.4 and is clamped to three steps, because the chest cross must survive as one bright shape rather than dissolve into a gradient. The previous version's three-tier value plan is load-bearing and is protected by an asymmetric clamp - a field the artist placed in the dark tier can only lose one step, a field in the light tier can only gain one - so darks/mids/lights still alternate vertically down the figure and the grayscale check still separates rust bib, dark belt, pale trousers, dark boots.

The head is exempt from the rules and authored by hand across rows 3-19: automatic edge lighting halos the eye and mouth ink and destroys the face. Wear is hand-placed as well, roughly 180 pixels of it - oxide bloom on the injector's steel spine and belt hardware, a chipped stencil edge and grime pooling at the bottom of the rust bib, worn paint on the cross's lower-right arm, dried mud caked at the boot hems, road dust on the trouser knees, a rubbed leather highlight on the belt's left end, tread notches in the boot soles, and a glass specular streak with a fluid meniscus in the injector charge window, which is now readable as a lit tube rather than a flat teal block.

Sacrifices. The frame is still full at 48px wide, so there is very little breathing room and interior negative space is limited to two 1px armpit slits. All of this added colour is authored for the 1x-to-6x range and is largely wasted below it; the extra steps do not add legibility at 28px, they only stop the sprite looking like flat vector shapes at native and above. The figure remains deliberately asymmetric and bottom-heavy, which suits a grounded, gritty read but makes it less suitable if the lineup needs a centred, symmetrical idle. And 55 colours is a real cost if this set ever has to share a hardware-style fixed palette - the ramps are internally consistent and could be quantised back to about 34 by dropping one step from each material, but not below that without losing the hue rotation that is the point of the pass.
frontFacingCue:
A fully lit front face plane with an explicit feature set - two 3px-wide ink eyes under a hard dark brow band, a 2px nose shadow, and a 4px mouth line - rendered in skin whose lit plane runs L138 (#b87c58) up to a single L215 cheekbone specular (#f2d3a6) against hair at L43, a 95-step separation that survives grayscale. The palette pass strengthened this cue rather than diluting it: the face is now modelled left-to-right across four skin steps (golden L177 rim on the upper-left cheek, L138 base, L109 half-tone across the far cheek and jaw, L75 shadow, with a single L46 plum-cool terminator column against the hair) so the head reads as a turned volume lit from the upper left rather than a flat mask, while the eye/nose/mouth ink is untouched and still the highest-contrast thing on the sprite. Crucially the shadow-side skin never gets dark enough to merge with the hair - the darkest skin step is L46 and the lightest hair step touching it is L43 only at the 1px boundary, so the head edge stays defined.

It is framed top and bottom by two more front-only reads: a pale headlamp band running straight across the brow, now itself a ramp from L245 at the left corner nearest the lamp down to L155 at the right temple with a grey-violet L108 underside, so the band reads as a cylinder wrapping the skull rather than a white sticker - and its lamp housing jutting out to the left with a two-pixel teal lens (L213 core, L244 hotspot) that is the only light source visibly present in frame, which is what justifies the whole upper-left lighting scheme. Below, a 4-row lit neck only 8px wide drops out of a 20px head into 26px shoulders, so the head demonstrably clears the shoulder line under the top-down dimetric camera. Nothing rises above the shoulders except the head. The chest cross, the bib straps and both hands are all frontal-plane elements, so the torso confirms the same facing the face does - the rejected version failed precisely here, burying a tiny face inside a hood blob that was the same width as the body with no neck at all.
smallCheck:
Honest verdict: it survives, reduced to three signals, and the palette pass neither helped nor hurt it much. I rendered a nearest-neighbour 21x28 downscale and inspected it magnified against the same downscale of the 24-colour version. What holds: the head reads as a head with a discernible dark eye band and the bright headlamp stripe anchoring it; the neck notch still separates head from shoulders; the chest cross is still the single strongest shape, though it degrades to a bright rounded blob rather than a legible cross; the injector reads as a dark tube with a teal core, and the new glass specular actually survives as one bright pixel that makes the tube read slightly better than before; the two legs stay separate and the boots anchor.

What is lost: essentially all of the new palette work. Dose ticks, buckle rivets, knuckle ridges, the stray hair strand, the stencil chipping, the mud at the boot hems, the oxide bloom on the injector spine and the tread notches in the soles all become stray single pixels or vanish outright. The extra value steps average out under nearest-neighbour sampling, so the figure lands almost exactly where the flat version did - the three-tier value plan is doing all the work at this size, and it is intact. The one genuine small-size regression is the trousers, which now sit about one step darker than before and separate slightly less from the boots; the one genuine gain is the headlamp band, whose left-to-right ramp keeps a bright pixel at the lamp end instead of a uniform bar.

The satchel still degrades worst: it survives as a rust mass but its small bone cross becomes a light smudge that competes with the chest cross rather than reinforcing it, and the left hand merges into the bag. The 1px armpit gaps close entirely, so the silhouette goes solid. If ~28px is the shipping size I would cut the satchel's cross marking, drop the ampoule bandolier to a plain dark band, quantise the sheet back to roughly a dozen colours, and hand-tune a dedicated small variant rather than downscale this one - a naive downscale now wastes closer to three quarters of the authored detail than half.
